concepts.title: Capturing Data
concepts.explanation: Before you can manage data, you have to capture it — that is, collect it. And before you collect it, you have to plan. Good data managers never just grab numbers randomly; they think carefully about what they want to find out and how they will find it out. This is called a statistical investigation. What is a statistical investigation? A statistical investigation is the collection of data to help you answer a question. For example, Maya might want to find out the mean (average) number of goals her team scores in a month. She would look at each match, write down the goals, and then work out the mean. Or Sami might want to find out how many different birds visit the school garden in one hour — he would sit and count them. Both of these are statistical investigations, because both collect data to answer a clear question. Not all data is the same. Knowing which type you are collecting helps you choose the right tool to collect it. There are three types you need to know. Here is the key difference to remember. Discrete data is counted and is always a whole number — you cannot have half a person in a room. Continuous data is measured and can be any value at all, like a temperature of 24.5 degrees or a height of 1.42 metres. Because continuous data can be so precise, capturing it needs extra care — and that is exactly what Sami's weather investigation needs. When you plan a statistical investigation, you should ask yourself six questions before you collect a single number. Answering them first saves you a lot of trouble later. What do I want to find out? For example, 'How does the temperature in Mogadishu change during the week?' What questions will help me find it out? Your questions must give you exactly the data you need. Who or what will I ask or measure? Be specific. 'The temperature outside our classroom' is specific; 'the temperature' is not. How will I collect the data? A questionnaire for opinions, a thermometer or data logger for temperature, and so on. How will I analyse the data? Perhaps with a spreadsheet, and a chart to make patterns easy to see. What tools will I use throughout? A data logger, a spreadsheet, a database, or a form — or a mixture. There is a range of computing tools you can use to capture data. Choosing the right one depends on the type of data and how you want to collect it. Data loggers — a device that uses sensors to record data over time, all by itself. A weather station that records the temperature and wind speed every hour is a data logger. Because it works on its own, it can be left in a hard-to-reach place, like a mountain top, for months. Data loggers are excellent for capturing continuous data. Spreadsheets — such as LibreOffice Calc. A spreadsheet stores data in a neat grid and can do calculations and draw charts. It is perfect for recording readings and then analysing them. Databases — such as LibreOffice Base. A database stores, organises and lets you search large amounts of organised data quickly. Forms and questionnaires — a series of questions people fill in. A form can be on paper, in a word processor, or an online form. Forms are great for collecting answers from many people. Every year there are between 12,000 and 14,000 earthquakes around the world.
concepts.example: They are measured by a special kind of data logger called a seismograph, which senses the tiny shaking of the ground and records it automatically, day and night, without anyone standing next to it.

concepts.title: Designing a form to collect continuous data
concepts.explanation: Continuous data can be tricky to capture, because it can be any value and it often changes over time. If you design a form to collect it, you must think carefully about five things, or your data will be messy and hard to use. Phrase your questions precisely. 'What was the temperature outside your classroom at 12:00 on Monday?' is precise. 'What is the temperature?' is not — it does not say where or when. How often should data be entered? If you want a reading three times a day, say so, and leave space for three readings each day. Over what period should data be entered? For a week? For a month? Make it clear and leave enough space. What measurements will you use? Degrees Celsius? Millimetres of rainfall? Kilograms? State the unit so everyone answers the same way. How precise should the data be? For example, you might ask for answers to one decimal place, like 24.5, not 24.5123. When you make a form, you choose a question type for each question — the way the question is asked and answered. Different types suit different data. Open text questions let people write their own answer, such as 'Why do you like reading?'. They are good for opinions, but people might answer in the wrong format. You can control this with validation rules, which only accept certain kinds of answer. Multiple choice questions let people pick from a set of answers, such as 'What is your favourite colour?'. They are quick, but they are not good for continuous data, because you would need a choice for every possible value — which is impossible. Ranking questions let people choose on a scale, such as 'Rate today's lunch from 1 to 5'. They are great for opinions, but they do not collect continuous or discrete data.
concepts.example: So which question type is best for collecting continuous data like temperature or height? An open text question with validation rules — such as a box that only accepts a number to one decimal place. This gives the precise, numerical answer you need while stopping people from typing nonsense.

concepts.title: Hands
concepts.explanation: You do not need an expensive online form to capture continuous data carefully. You can build a smart data-capture sheet in LibreOffice Calc, and use its validation rules to make sure only sensible answers are accepted. This is exactly what Sami needs for his Mogadishu weather investigation. Here is how the sheet is set out: To stop anyone typing a word or a silly number into the rainfall column, Sami adds a validation rule. He selects the cells B2:B8, then opens the menu Data > Validity. On the Criteria tab he sets Allow to Decimal, the condition to between, a Minimum of 0 and a Maximum of 500. Now the cells will only accept a decimal number from 0 to 500 — a real rainfall reading. On the Error Alert tab he chooses the Stop action, so a wrong entry is refused with a friendly message. For categorical data, like the type of weather, validation can give a drop-down list instead. Sami selects a column, opens Data > Validity, sets Allow to List, and types the choices Sunny, Cloudy, Rainy and Windy, one per line. Now that column shows a neat drop-down arrow, and no one can misspell 'Sunny' or invent a new category by accident. That is a validation rule doing its job. It is usually an opinion, a description, or a range. · Favourite colour, type of pet, favourite lesson, age group 7-11. · Day · Rainfall (mm) Discrete — Numerical data that can only be whole numbers. You often count it, and you cannot have half. · Number of learners in a class, number of customers, number of goals. · Saturday · 1.2
concepts.example: Continuous — Numerical data that can take ANY value, including decimals. You usually measure it, not count it. · Temperature, height, weight, rainfall, the time taken to run a race. · Sunday · 3.4

concepts.title: Creating a Spreadsheet
concepts.explanation: Now that you can capture data, it is time to organise and analyse it. The best tool for numerical data is a spreadsheet, and you will use LibreOffice Calc. A spreadsheet is far more than a place to store numbers — it is a powerful calculator that can work on thousands of numbers at once and never makes an arithmetic mistake. A spreadsheet is a document split into a large grid. Each little box in the grid is called a cell. The cells are organised into rows, which go across, and columns, which go down. Each row has a unique number (1, 2, 3, ...) and each column has a unique letter (A, B, C, ...). 'Unique' means one of a kind — there is only one row 3 and only one column B, just as there is only one of you. When you open LibreOffice Calc, look for these parts of the screen: The Name Box at the top-left corner, which shows the reference of the cell you have selected. The Input Line (the formula bar) next to it, where you can see and type what is inside a cell. The sheet tabs at the bottom (Sheet1, Sheet2, ...). One file can hold many sheets. The AutoSum button, marked with the Greek letter sigma, which quickly adds up a column or row for you. Every cell has an address made of its column letter and its row number. This is called a cell reference. The letter tells you the column (how far across), and the number tells you the row (how far down). So the cell where column B meets row 3 has the cell reference B3. Cell references are the secret to a spreadsheet's power. Instead of typing a number into a calculation, you type the cell reference where that number lives. Then, if you ever change the number in that cell, every calculation that uses it updates automatically. It is like magic, but it is really just clever organisation. To make a calculation in a spreadsheet, you write a formula. A formula is an instruction to do a calculation, and it always begins with an equals sign =. The = tells LibreOffice Calc, 'Do not treat this as ordinary text — work this out for me.' Formulas combine cell references with arithmetic operators, the symbols we use for maths: For example, =C3*D4 multiplies the value in cell C3 by the value in cell D4. If C3 holds 2 and D4 holds 4, the formula returns 8. One golden rule: always put a formula in a separate cell — not in either of the cells you are using in the calculation. You can type a formula straight into an empty cell, or click the cell and type into the Input Line at the top. A function is a ready-made calculation that is already built into LibreOffice Calc. Each function has a name, and you 'call' it by that name. Functions save you from writing very long formulas. There are more than 500 functions in Calc, but in this unit you will focus on two: SUM and AVERAGE.
concepts.example: To use a function you follow three steps: start with =, then the function name, then the cell references inside brackets. Inside the brackets you use a colon : to mean 'to'. So A1:A10 means 'from cell A1 to cell A10, and everything in between'.

concepts.title: Worked example: Aunt Amara's shop in Hargeisa
concepts.explanation:
Let us help Aunt Amara. She sells school items in her Hargeisa shop, and she has told you the price of each item and how many she sold this week, all in Somali shillings. You type her data into LibreOffice Calc like this:

Column D works out the total money from each item by multiplying its price by the number sold. In cell D2 you type =B2*C2 and press Enter. The result is 30000, because 2000 multiplied by 15 is 30000. You do not have to type the formula seven times, though. You can click D2, then use the Fill Down shortcut Ctrl+D (or the menu Sheet > Fill Cells > Down) to copy the formula down to D8. LibreOffice cleverly changes the cell references for each row, so D3 becomes =B3*C3, and so on. Here are all the results:

Column D: total money from each item

Now Amara wants three big answers: her total sales, the total number of items she sold, and the average price of an item. You put each in a separate cell using SUM and AVERAGE:
concepts.example: Total number of items sold: in C9 type =SUM(C2:C8) -> 61

concepts.title: Total sales in shillings
concepts.explanation: Average price per item: in B11 type =AVERAGE(B2:B8) -> 8000 Let us check those by hand so you can see the software is right. The numbers sold are 15, 20, 8, 5, 6, 4 and 3, which add up to 61. The item totals in column D are 30000, 60000, 40000, 40000, 60000, 48000 and 48000, which add up to 326000 shillings. And the seven prices are 2000, 3000, 5000, 8000, 10000, 12000 and 16000, which add up to 56000; divide by 7 and you get an average price of 8000 shillings. Amara is delighted — what would have taken her an hour with a paper and pencil took LibreOffice Calc less than a second. A modern LibreOffice Calc sheet has 1,048,576 rows and up to 16,384 columns. That is more than 17 billion cells in a single sheet — far more than anyone could ever fill by hand. Calc also has more than 500 built-in functions, each one a ready-made calculation waiting for you to use it. Real spreadsheets often hold huge amounts of data. The skill of a good data manager is selecting just the pieces you need to answer a question. To select data for a calculation in LibreOffice Calc you can either type the cell references into your formula, or click and drag across the cells you want. When you drag, Calc fills the range into your formula for you. Imagine Sami's weather sheet holds a whole month of readings: maximum temperature, minimum temperature, humidity and rainfall. To find the mean maximum temperature for the month, he selects only the maximum-temperature column and uses AVERAGE on it. He would not try to average the wind direction, because 'north' and 'east' are categorical words, not numbers — you cannot calculate a mean of them. Choosing the right data is just as important as choosing the right formula. Numbers in a grid are useful, but a chart makes patterns jump out at you. To turn Amara's data into a chart in LibreOffice Calc: Select the data you want to show. For a chart of each item's total, select the Item column and the Total column together (A1:A8 and D1:D8). Open the menu Insert > Chart. The Chart Wizard appears. Step 1 — Choose a Chart Type. Pick Column for tall bars, or Bar for sideways bars. Click Next. Step 2 and 3 — Data Range and Data Series. Check that 'First row as label' and 'First column as label' are ticked, then click Next. Step 4 — Chart Elements. Type a Title such as 'Shop sales this week', label the axes, and tick Display legend. Click Finish. Click anywhere outside the chart to leave edit mode. Your chart is done! Now anyone can see at a glance that the water bottle and the exercise book brought in the most money, while the pen brought in the least. That is the power of turning data into a picture. Just as you planned your form in 2.1, you should plan a spreadsheet before you build it. Ask yourself: What data will I use? What headings will the columns have? How will I organise it so it is easy to understand? What format will the data be in? What calculations do I want to do, and which formulas or functions will do them? A few minutes of planning saves a lot of tidying up later. concepts.title: Creating a Database
concepts.explanation: A spreadsheet is wonderful for calculations. But when you want to store, organise and search a lot of information — like every book in the school library — a database is even better. In this subunit you will design a database, build it in LibreOffice Base, and learn to search it in seconds. This is exactly what the librarian, Nadia, needs. A database is an organised set of data. It is useful because organised data is so much easier to use than a messy pile. A database is made up of records and fields. A record is all the data about one thing. In a library database, one book is one record. A field is a category of data within a record. For a book, the fields might be Title, Author, Category and Year. An attribute is the actual piece of data in one field of one record — for example, the Title attribute of one particular book might be 'Somali Folk Tales'. In a database, records are usually shown as rows and fields as columns — just like a spreadsheet grid. A record is complete when every field is filled in. Here is Nadia's library database, with six book records: Look at record number 4. Its fields are BookID, Title, Author, Category, Year and 'On loan?'. Its attributes are 4, 'Somali Folk Tales', 'Dina Ali', 'Story', 2018 and 'No'. If Nadia wanted to know who wrote 'Somali Folk Tales', she would look at the Author field of that record and find the attribute 'Dina Ali'. Every field stores a particular kind, or type, of data. Choosing the right data type keeps your database tidy and correct. Here are the main types you need to know. For example, think of a record about a country: Country: Oman (a string of text), Size: 309500 km2 (an integer), Population: 4576298 (an integer), Language: Arabic (text), Currency: Omani rial (a string). In Nadia's library database, the BookID and Year fields are integers, the Title, Author and Category fields are text, and the 'On loan?' field is a special Yes/No type. Sometimes we want data to *look* a certain way. Formatting controls how the data is displayed — without changing the real value underneath. In LibreOffice you format cells by selecting them and opening Format > Cells (the shortcut is Ctrl+1). concepts.title: Shows as 1/2
concepts.explanation: When you first type into a cell, LibreOffice treats it as 'General' and guesses the format for you — type $5 and it becomes currency. But it is safer to set the format yourself with Format > Cells, especially for integers (whole numbers) that should not show a decimal point. Before you build a database, you design it on paper. Good designers ask these questions first: What records will there be, and how many? (Each book is a record.) What fields does each record need? (Title, Author, Category, and so on.) What data type suits each field? (Text for the title, integer for the year.) What will the column titles be? Will the database be on paper or digital?

concepts.title: Creating the database in LibreOffice Base
concepts.explanation: You can build a simple database inside a spreadsheet (headings as fields, rows as records), and that is fine for very small jobs. But the proper tool is LibreOffice Base, which is built only for databases. Here is how Nadia creates her library database. Open LibreOffice and choose Base Database, or use the menu File > New > Database. The Database Wizard opens. Choose Create a new database and click Next. Leave the registration choice as it is, keep Open the database for editing ticked, and click Finish. LibreOffice asks where to save the file. Give it a name like library and save it (it becomes library.odb). In the left-hand panel, click Tables, then click Create Table in Design View. For each field, type a Field Name (such as BookID, Title, Author, Category, Year, OnLoan) and choose a Field Type from the drop-down. Set the data types: BookID as Integer [INTEGER], Title, Author and Category as Text [VARCHAR], Year as Integer [INTEGER], and OnLoan as Yes/No [BOOLEAN]. Make BookID the primary key (the field that gives every record a unique number): right-click the small grey box to the left of the BookID row and choose Primary Key. Save the table with Ctrl+S and name it Books. Double-click the Books table to open it, then type in your six records, one row at a time. A primary key is important: it is a field, like BookID, that is unique for every record. It means the database can always tell two records apart, even if two different books had the same title. Once your records are typed in, you have a real, working, digital database. Well done! Phrase searching — searching for data that matches a whole series of words, such as a full title or a full name. This finds exactly the record you want. A first name alone might match several people, but a full name is far more precise. Filtering — using a filter to hide every record that does not meet your criteria, so only the records you want are shown. To do a phrase search in LibreOffice Base, open the Books table and click the Find Record tool (the binoculars icon). Type the phrase Somali Folk Tales, and Base jumps straight to that record. To search inside a LibreOffice Calc database instead, you would use Edit > Find & Replace (the shortcut is Ctrl+H), or the Find toolbar with Ctrl+F, and type your phrase. To filter in LibreOffice Base, use the filter tools on the toolbar or the Data menu. For example, filtering the Category field for Poetry would show only records 2 and 6. Filtering the 'OnLoan' field for Yes would show only the books currently borrowed — records 3 and 6 — which is exactly how Nadia checks which books are out. A single search that once took Nadia half an hour now takes half a second.

concepts.title: How Is Data Used?
concepts.explanation: You now know how to capture data, calculate with it, and store it in a database. But why do people go to all this trouble? Because organised data helps us solve real problems. By looking closely at data we can spot trends — patterns that show how often something happens or how things change over time. Once you can see a trend, you can make a smart decision. Using data to solve problems in retail Retail means selling things to people — clothes, food, cars, games. A shop can use its sales data to solve problems like not selling enough or not having enough customers. Let us look at Leila's Cafe, which recorded its customers and takings (in shillings) for one week: Putting this in LibreOffice Calc, the owner can find the total customers with =SUM(B2:B8), which is 260, and the total takings with =SUM(C2:C8), which is 1300000 shillings. To find the average spend per customer she divides the total takings by the total customers: =C9/B9 gives 5000 shillings per customer. But the most useful thing the data shows is a trend: Friday is the busiest day (55 customers) and Tuesday is the quietest (25). Now the owner knows to prepare extra food for Friday, and perhaps offer a special deal on Tuesday to attract more people. That is data solving a real problem. A shop manager can also look at which products sell well and which do not. They might stop stocking the least popular items, order more of the popular ones, or lower the price of items that have not sold for a long time. Every one of those decisions is made better by looking at the data first. Using data to solve problems in healthcare Healthcare means looking after people's medical needs. Data helps doctors find the best treatments, spot new illnesses, reduce waiting times, and ultimately save more lives. Imagine doctors testing two medicines for a new illness. Each patient is given a wellness score out of 10 before treatment, and again two months later. The improvement is the 'after' score minus the 'before' score. The average improvement for Treatment A is 4 points, while for Treatment B it is only 1.5 points. The data tells a clear story: Treatment A works far better, so the hospital should choose it. Notice that the doctors could not have known this without carefully recording and comparing the data. This is how medical trials really work, and it is how new cures are discovered. Using data to solve problems in manufacturing Manufacturing means making large numbers of goods in a factory. Data can help a factory make better products, sell more, and — very importantly — keep its workers safe. Suppose a workshop in Mogadishu recorded where accidents happened over one month: The data reveals a clear trend: the welding area has by far the most accidents (8), followed by the cutting area (5). The factory owner can now use this data in at least three ways: to focus safety training and new equipment on the welding area first; to check whether the welding machines need repair; and to set a goal of reducing welding accidents next month and measure whether it worked. Fewer accidents keep workers safe and also save the business money, because injured staff and stopped machines are expensive. In every example — the shop, the hospital, the factory — the pattern is the same. Someone had a problem, they collected organised data, they looked for trends, and the trends pointed to a solution. That is the whole reason we manage data. Numbers are not the goal; better decisions are the goal. Large supermarkets record every single item sold, every hour of every day. By studying trends in this data, they can predict how much bread or how many mangoes they will sell next week, so the shelves are never empty and very little food is wasted. That is millions of decisions guided by data. workedExamples.title: Worked example 1: Capturing Data
workedExamples.prompt: Which of these is continuous data? (a) Number of pets (b) Favourite colour (c) Temperature (d) Number of goals
workedExamples.solution: Before you can manage data, you have to capture it — that is, collect it. And before you collect it, you have to plan. Good data managers never just grab numbers randomly; they think carefully about what they want to find out and how they will find it out. This is called a statistical investigation. What is a statistical investigation? A statistical investigation is the collection of data to help you answer a question. For example, Maya might want to find out the mean (average) number of goals her team scores in a month. She would look at each match, write down the goals, and then work out the mean. Or Sami might want to find out how many different birds visit the school garden in one hour — he would sit and count them. Both of these are statistical investigations, because both collect data to answer a clear question. Not all data is the same. Knowing which type you are collecting helps you choose the right tool to collect it. There are three types you need to know. Here is the key difference to remember. Discrete data is counted and is always a whole number — you cannot have half a person in a room. Continuous data is measured and can be any value at all, like a temperature of 24.5 degrees or a height of 1.42 metres. Because continuous data can be so precise, capturing it needs extra care — and that is exactly what Sami's weather investigation needs. When you plan a statistical investigation, you should ask yourself six questions before you collect a single number. Answering them first saves you a lot of trouble later. What do I want to find out? For example, 'How does the temperature in Mogadishu change during the week?' What questions will help me find it out? Your questions must give you exactly the data you need. Who or what will I ask or measure? Be specific. 'The temperature outside our classroom' is specific; 'the temperature' is not. How will I collect the data? A questionnaire for opinions, a thermometer or data logger for temperature, and so on. How will I analyse the data? Perhaps with a spreadsheet, and a chart to make patterns easy to see. What tools will I use throughout? A data logger, a spreadsheet, a database, or a form — or a mixture. There is a range of computing tools you can use to capture data. Choosing the right one depends on the type of data and how you want to collect it. Data loggers — a device that uses sensors to record data over time, all by itself. A weather station that records the temperature and wind speed every hour is a data logger. Because it works on its own, it can be left in a hard-to-reach place, like a mountain top, for months. Data loggers are excellent for capturing continuous data. Spreadsheets — such as LibreOffice Calc. A spreadsheet stores data in a neat grid and can do calculations and draw charts. It is perfect for recording readings and then analysing them. Databases — such as LibreOffice Base. A database stores, organises and lets you search large amounts of organised data quickly. Forms and questionnaires — a series of questions people fill in. A form can be on paper, in a word processor, or an online form. Forms are great for collecting answers from many people. Every year there are between 12,000 and 14,000 earthquakes around the world. For example: They are measured by a special kind of data logger called a seismograph, which senses the tiny shaking of the ground and records it automatically, day and night, without anyone standing next to it.

workedExamples.title: Worked example 2: Designing a form to collect continuous data
workedExamples.prompt: A statistical investigation is: (a) A type of chart (b) Collecting data to answer a question (c) A spreadsheet formula (d) A kind of database
workedExamples.solution: Continuous data can be tricky to capture, because it can be any value and it often changes over time. If you design a form to collect it, you must think carefully about five things, or your data will be messy and hard to use. Phrase your questions precisely. 'What was the temperature outside your classroom at 12:00 on Monday?' is precise. 'What is the temperature?' is not — it does not say where or when. How often should data be entered? If you want a reading three times a day, say so, and leave space for three readings each day. Over what period should data be entered? For a week? For a month? Make it clear and leave enough space. What measurements will you use? Degrees Celsius? Millimetres of rainfall? Kilograms? State the unit so everyone answers the same way. How precise should the data be? For example, you might ask for answers to one decimal place, like 24.5, not 24.5123. When you make a form, you choose a question type for each question — the way the question is asked and answered. Different types suit different data. Open text questions let people write their own answer, such as 'Why do you like reading?'. They are good for opinions, but people might answer in the wrong format. You can control this with validation rules, which only accept certain kinds of answer. Multiple choice questions let people pick from a set of answers, such as 'What is your favourite colour?'. They are quick, but they are not good for continuous data, because you would need a choice for every possible value — which is impossible. Ranking questions let people choose on a scale, such as 'Rate today's lunch from 1 to 5'. They are great for opinions, but they do not collect continuous or discrete data. For example: So which question type is best for collecting continuous data like temperature or height? An open text question with validation rules — such as a box that only accepts a number to one decimal place. This gives the precise, numerical answer you need while stopping people from typing nonsense.

workedExamples.title: Worked example 3: Hands
workedExamples.prompt: A data logger is best for collecting: (a) Opinions (b) Categories (c) Continuous data over time (d) Names
workedExamples.solution: You do not need an expensive online form to capture continuous data carefully. You can build a smart data-capture sheet in LibreOffice Calc, and use its validation rules to make sure only sensible answers are accepted. This is exactly what Sami needs for his Mogadishu weather investigation. Here is how the sheet is set out: To stop anyone typing a word or a silly number into the rainfall column, Sami adds a validation rule. He selects the cells B2:B8, then opens the menu Data > Validity. On the Criteria tab he sets Allow to Decimal, the condition to between, a Minimum of 0 and a Maximum of 500. Now the cells will only accept a decimal number from 0 to 500 — a real rainfall reading. On the Error Alert tab he chooses the Stop action, so a wrong entry is refused with a friendly message. For categorical data, like the type of weather, validation can give a drop-down list instead. Sami selects a column, opens Data > Validity, sets Allow to List, and types the choices Sunny, Cloudy, Rainy and Windy, one per line. Now that column shows a neat drop-down arrow, and no one can misspell 'Sunny' or invent a new category by accident. That is a validation rule doing its job. You often count it, and you cannot have half. · Number of learners in a class, number of customers, number of goals. · Saturday · 1.2 For example: Continuous — Numerical data that can take ANY value, including decimals. workedExamples.title: Worked example 4: Creating a Spreadsheet
workedExamples.prompt: Every spreadsheet formula must begin with: (a) A colon (b) An equals sign (c) A bracket (d) A letter
workedExamples.solution: Now that you can capture data, it is time to organise and analyse it. The best tool for numerical data is a spreadsheet, and you will use LibreOffice Calc. A spreadsheet is far more than a place to store numbers — it is a powerful calculator that can work on thousands of numbers at once and never makes an arithmetic mistake. A spreadsheet is a document split into a large grid. Each little box in the grid is called a cell. The cells are organised into rows, which go across, and columns, which go down. Each row has a unique number (1, 2, 3, ...) and each column has a unique letter (A, B, C, ...). 'Unique' means one of a kind — there is only one row 3 and only one column B, just as there is only one of you. When you open LibreOffice Calc, look for these parts of the screen: The Name Box at the top-left corner, which shows the reference of the cell you have selected. The Input Line (the formula bar) next to it, where you can see and type what is inside a cell. The sheet tabs at the bottom (Sheet1, Sheet2, ...). One file can hold many sheets. The AutoSum button, marked with the Greek letter sigma, which quickly adds up a column or row for you. Every cell has an address made of its column letter and its row number. This is called a cell reference. The letter tells you the column (how far across), and the number tells you the row (how far down). So the cell where column B meets row 3 has the cell reference B3. Cell references are the secret to a spreadsheet's power. Instead of typing a number into a calculation, you type the cell reference where that number lives. Then, if you ever change the number in that cell, every calculation that uses it updates automatically. It is like magic, but it is really just clever organisation. To make a calculation in a spreadsheet, you write a formula. A formula is an instruction to do a calculation, and it always begins with an equals sign =. The = tells LibreOffice Calc, 'Do not treat this as ordinary text — work this out for me.' Formulas combine cell references with arithmetic operators, the symbols we use for maths: For example, =C3*D4 multiplies the value in cell C3 by the value in cell D4. If C3 holds 2 and D4 holds 4, the formula returns 8. One golden rule: always put a formula in a separate cell — not in either of the cells you are using in the calculation. You can type a formula straight into an empty cell, or click the cell and type into the Input Line at the top. A function is a ready-made calculation that is already built into LibreOffice Calc. Each function has a name, and you 'call' it by that name. Functions save you from writing very long formulas. There are more than 500 functions in Calc, but in this unit you will focus on two: SUM and AVERAGE. For example: To use a function you follow three steps: start with =, then the function name, then the cell references inside brackets. Inside the brackets you use a colon : to mean 'to'. So A1:A10 means 'from cell A1 to cell A10, and everything in between'.

workedExamples.prompt: Which formula correctly adds the values from B2 to B8? (a) =SUMB2:B8 (b) SUM(B2:B8) (c) =SUM(B2:B8) (d) =SUM(B2-B8)
workedExamples.solution: Average price per item: in B11 type =AVERAGE(B2:B8) -> 8000 Let us check those by hand so you can see the software is right. The numbers sold are 15, 20, 8, 5, 6, 4 and 3, which add up to 61. The item totals in column D are 30000, 60000, 40000, 40000, 60000, 48000 and 48000, which add up to 326000 shillings. And the seven prices are 2000, 3000, 5000, 8000, 10000, 12000 and 16000, which add up to 56000; divide by 7 and you get an average price of 8000 shillings. Amara is delighted — what would have taken her an hour with a paper and pencil took LibreOffice Calc less than a second. A modern LibreOffice Calc sheet has 1,048,576 rows and up to 16,384 columns. That is more than 17 billion cells in a single sheet — far more than anyone could ever fill by hand. Calc also has more than 500 built-in functions, each one a ready-made calculation waiting for you to use it. Real spreadsheets often hold huge amounts of data. The skill of a good data manager is selecting just the pieces you need to answer a question. To select data for a calculation in LibreOffice Calc you can either type the cell references into your formula, or click and drag across the cells you want. When you drag, Calc fills the range into your formula for you. Imagine Sami's weather sheet holds a whole month of readings: maximum temperature, minimum temperature, humidity and rainfall. To find the mean maximum temperature for the month, he selects only the maximum-temperature column and uses AVERAGE on it. He would not try to average the wind direction, because 'north' and 'east' are categorical words, not numbers — you cannot calculate a mean of them. Choosing the right data is just as important as choosing the right formula. Numbers in a grid are useful, but a chart makes patterns jump out at you. To turn Amara's data into a chart in LibreOffice Calc: Select the data you want to show. For a chart of each item's total, select the Item column and the Total column together (A1:A8 and D1:D8). Open the menu Insert > Chart. The Chart Wizard appears. Step 1 — Choose a Chart Type. Pick Column for tall bars, or Bar for sideways bars. Click Next. Step 2 and 3 — Data Range and Data Series. Check that 'First row as label' and 'First column as label' are ticked, then click Next. Step 4 — Chart Elements. Type a Title such as 'Shop sales this week', label the axes, and tick Display legend. Click Finish. Click anywhere outside the chart to leave edit mode. Your chart is done! Now anyone can see at a glance that the water bottle and the exercise book brought in the most money, while the pen brought in the least. That is the power of turning data into a picture. Just as you planned your form in 2.1, you should plan a spreadsheet before you build it. Ask yourself: What data will I use? What headings will the columns have? How will I organise it so it is easy to understand? What format will the data be in? What calculations do I want to do, and which formulas or functions will do them? A few minutes of planning saves a lot of tidying up later. rules.title: Remember
rules.text: Every formula starts with an equals sign: =SUM(B2:B8). In a spreadsheet, * means multiply and / means divide. The colon : means 'to', so B2:B8 means every cell from B2 to B8.

rules.title: Remember
rules.text: SUM adds up the selected cells. AVERAGE finds the mean of the selected cells. Only use AVERAGE on numbers, never on words like 'north' or 'Sunny'. Put your formula in an empty cell, not in a cell you are calculating with.

rules.title: Remember
rules.text: In a database, records are rows (one thing) and fields are columns (categories). An attribute is one value, in one field, of one record. A primary key is a field that is unique for every record.

rules.title: Remember
rules.text: Continuous data is measured and can be any value; discrete data is counted and is always whole. A validation rule keeps bad data out and lets good data in. A trend is a pattern in data, and patterns help us solve problems.

rules.title: Remember
rules.text: Validation rules are like a helpful gatekeeper: they let good data in and keep bad data out. Data > Validity in LibreOffice Calc can force a cell to accept only whole numbers, only decimals, only dates, only times, or only items from a list. The Stop action refuses a wrong entry completely; a Warning or Information action lets it in but warns the user first.

rules.title: Remember
rules.text: Every formula must start with an equals sign. No equals sign, no calculation! In a spreadsheet, * means multiply and / means divide. Put your formula in a cell of its own, not in a cell that holds one of the numbers you are calculating with. Functions: SUM and AVERAGE A function is a ready-made calculation that is already built into LibreOffice Calc. Each function has a name, and you 'call' it by that name. Functions save you from writing very long formulas. There are more than 500 functions in Calc, but in this unit you will focus on two: SUM and AVERAGE. To use a function you follow three steps: start with =, then the function name, then the cell references inside brackets. Inside the brackets you use a colon : to mean 'to'. So A1:A10 means 'from cell A1 to cell A10, and everything in between'.

rules.title: Remember
rules.text: Fields are the columns (the categories, like Title or Author). Records are the rows (all the data about one thing, like one book). An attribute is one piece of data — the value in one field of one record. A primary key is a field that is unique for every record, so no two records can be confused. Searching a database The best thing about a database is how quickly it finds information. Searching organised data is far faster than reading through a pile of paper cards. There are three main ways to search.
